lesson.title: The Feminine Squad
lesson.subtitle: -ung, -heit, -keit drills: derive abstract nouns and their genders

hook.title: The Noun Factory With One Gender
hook.content: German builds abstract nouns on an assembly line, and the line stamps one gender: feminine. Verb + -ung: warnen → die Warnung, wandern → die Wanderung. Adjective + -heit: gesund → die Gesundheit (health). Adjective + -keit: möglich → die Möglichkeit (possibility). Noun + -schaft: wissen → die Wissenschaft (knowledge-ship, science). English used to run the same factory with -ness and -ship — 'friendship' is -schaft's sister suffix — but German never closed the line.

footnotes.title: The -ung Rule Has No Exceptions
footnotes.content: Every single -ung noun in German is feminine. No committee, no exceptions, no history of drift. It is the most reliable gender law in the language — and it works on verbs you have never seen: meet a new verb, add -ung, collect die.

pattern.title: Four Stamps, Fifteen Nouns
pattern.content: Stamp one, verb + -ung: warnen → die Warnung, wandern → die Wanderung (the hike), bilden → die Bildung (education). Stamp two, adjective + -heit: gesund → die Gesundheit, schön → die Schönheit (beauty), wahr → die Wahrheit (truth — the same wahr as in Wahrnehmung, 'truth-taking'!). Stamp three, adjective + -keit: möglich → die Möglichkeit, freundlich → die Freundlichkeit (friendliness). Stamp four, noun + -schaft: wissen → die Wissenschaft, Freund → die Freundschaft (friendship — English's own suffix, fossilized). Derivation recipe: chop the verb's -en or the adjective's bare form, glue the stamp, collect die.
pattern.linguist_note: -heit/-keit/-ung nouns are almost all Latin-era calque technology — Wahrnehmung, Wissenschaft and Gesundheit were built or rebuilt when German scholars translated Latin scholarship. The feminine gender rode in with the suffixes.

exercises.prompt: Factory check: what gender does -schaft stamp?
exercises.explanation: knowledge-ship and friend-ship are both die — and English's own '-ship' is the sister suffix. die Zeitung already wears the -ung twin of this law.

exercises.prompt: Run stamp one: 'wandern' → the -ung noun (the hike):
exercises.explanation: Chop -en, glue -ung: die Wanderung. Your hiking verb now has a noun form — feminine, by law.

exercises.prompt: Which noun does the -heit stamp produce from 'gesund' (healthy)?
exercises.explanation: Adjective + -heit → feminine abstract noun. Gesundheit — the word you say when someone sneezes.

exercises.prompt: Match each stamped noun with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: die Warnung, die Wahrheit, die Möglichkeit, die Wissenschaft, die Rechnung, die Blume, die Lampe, die Bluse
exercises.meaning: the warning, the truth, the possibility, the science, the bill, the flower, the lamp, the blouse
exercises.explanation: Four stamps, one gender — the entire feminine abstract factory in four words, and four plain-die nouns (Rechnung, Blume, Lampe, Bluse) marching in step.

exercises.meaning: Die Wahrheit ist gut = The truth is good
exercises.explanation: wahr (true) + -heit → die Wahrheit — the feminine squad carrying a philosophical sentence. (der Berg and das Flugzeug stay outside — no feminine suffix, no membership.)

summary.outcome: Derive -ung/-heit/-keit/-schaft nouns and stamp die on them automatically.
summary.takeaway: Four suffix stamps — -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft — build abstract nouns, and every one arrives feminine.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Guess-the-Gender Game — unseen words, suffix laws, explanation feedback.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We warn here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir warnen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in The Feminine Squad.

warnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *warnōn — a parallel formation to English warn (Old English wearnian). [wiktionary]

wahrnehmung.etymology_derivation: Calque of Latin perceptio (wahr = true + nehmen = take → taking as true).

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

rechnung.etymology_derivation: rechnen + -ung — the twin of English reckoning; the entry lists English reckoning as a cognate. [wiktionary]

blume.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *blōmō 'blossom'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

lampe.context_phrase: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.
lampe.context_translation: The lamp is on the table.
lampe.etymology_derivation: From Latin lampada — the same Latin loan as English lamp. [wiktionary]

bluse.context_phrase: Die Bluse ist weiß und die Hose ist schwarz.
bluse.context_translation: The blouse is white and the trousers are black.
bluse.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French blouse - the same French word that gave English blouse. [wiktionary]

zeitung.context_phrase: Er liest jeden Morgen die Zeitung.
zeitung.context_translation: He reads the newspaper every morning.
zeitung.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *tidungu, a message on the time-root — the page lists English tiding as the cognate: a Zeitung brings your tidings. [wiktionary]

berg.context_phrase: Der Berg ist im Winter weiß.
berg.context_translation: The mountain is white in winter.
berg.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bërg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz. English barrow, a burial hill, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

flugzeug.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly) + Zeug (gear, as in Feuerzeug): the fly-gear. [wiktionary]

briefmarke.etymology_derivation: Brief (the twin of brief, both from Latin brevis, short) + Marke (the twin of mark, both from Germanic mark-, sign) — a letter-mark, that is, a postage stamp. [wiktionary]

wolle.context_phrase: Der Schal ist aus warmer Wolle.
wolle.context_translation: The scarf is made of warm wool.
wolle.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *wullu - the exact twin of English wool, from the PIE root *h₂welh₁- (wool). [wiktionary]

außerdem.etymology_derivation: Außer (outside of, built on aus — out, twin of English out) plus dem (that); literally besides that. English besides is unrelated. [wiktionary]

staat.etymology_derivation: From Latin status via Old French estat, the same loan as English state; a doublet of German Status and Etat. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
